title: Diagonal Sums

concept.title: Diagonals are index patterns
body: In a square matrix of size `n` the **main diagonal** holds the cells where row and column are equal: `g[i][i]`. The **anti-diagonal** runs from the top right to the bottom left: row `i` meets column `n - 1 - i`.

body.code:
main = sum(g[i][i] for i in range(n))
anti = sum(g[i][n - 1 - i] for i in range(n))

body: One loop over `i` is enough. You never need to look at the other cells.

statement: Given a square matrix of size `n`, print the sum of the main diagonal and the sum of the anti-diagonal. If `n` is odd, the centre cell belongs to both diagonals and is counted in both sums.
inputFormat: The next `n` lines have `n` integers each.
outputFormat: Print the two sums separated by a space.
hints: One loop over i adds one cell to each sum.

starter.python:
n = int(input())
g = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]

# Your code here

explanation: Cell `(i, i)` is on the main diagonal and cell `(i, n-1-i)` is on the anti-diagonal. One loop adds both.

code.python:
n = int(input())
g = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(n)]

main = 0
anti = 0
for i in range(n):
    main += g[i][i]
    anti += g[i][n - 1 - i]
print(main, anti)
